sections.h2: Does Utah have its own capital gains tax on a house sale?
sections.html:
No. Utah does not run a separate capital gains tax, so any taxable gain from selling a house is simply part of your income and taxed at the state's flat individual income tax rate.

The 2025 TC-40 instructions put that rate at 4.5 percent, down from 4.55 percent after the 2025 Legislature passed HB 106. Line 4 of the Utah return starts from your federal adjusted gross income, which already includes any gain you report on your federal return. So the question for a Utah seller is mostly a federal one: how much of the gain survives the home sale exclusion?

Check the instructions for the year you sell, because the rate is set by the Legislature and can change from one tax year to the next.

sections.h2: How much gain can a Utah homeowner exclude?
sections.html:
A single seller can exclude up to $250,000 of gain on a main home, and married couples filing jointly can exclude up to $500,000.

The IRS requires that you meet two tests during the five years before the sale, each over 24 months, and the two periods do not have to match. For a joint return, either spouse can meet the ownership test but both must meet the use test. You generally cannot claim the exclusion if you took it on another home sale in the prior two years.

RuleFigure from the IRS
Exclusion, singleUp to $250,000
Exclusion, married filing jointlyUp to $500,000
Ownership test24 months within the last 5 years
Use as main home24 months (730 days) within the last 5 years
Look-backNo other home sale excluded in the prior 2 years

A surviving spouse can keep the $500,000 limit when the sale happens within two years of the spouse's death and the other conditions are met. The details are in IRS Publication 523.

sections.h2: How do you work out the gain on a Utah house?
sections.html:
Gain is the sale price minus selling expenses, minus your adjusted basis, which is what you paid plus qualifying improvements.

  • Amount realized: the selling price less selling expenses.
  • Basis: the purchase cost plus improvements that add value, prolong the home's life or adapt it to a new use. Repairs count only as part of a larger improvement project.
  • Closing costs: items such as recording fees, survey fees and owner's title insurance can be added to basis. Mortgage points and loan fees cannot.
  • Inherited homes: basis is generally the fair market value on the date of death, or on the alternate valuation date if the estate chose it.
  • Gifted homes: basis is generally the donor's adjusted basis.

Keep the closing statement from your original purchase and receipts for any addition, new roof or remodel. A finished basement or a new roof can change the taxable number noticeably, and a CPA can tie the figures together before you list.

sections.h2: When does the exclusion fall short?
sections.html:
The exclusion does not cover rental depreciation, periods when the house was not your main home, or a separate business portion of the property.

Publication 523 says depreciation adjustments taken after May 6, 1997 for business or rental use must be recaptured, and you cannot exclude the part of gain equal to them. Gain tied to nonqualified use after 2008, when the property was not your main home, generally cannot be excluded either. Depreciation recapture goes on Form 4797.

A partial exclusion is available if you sold before reaching 24 months for a qualifying reason:

  • A work move at least 50 miles farther from the home.
  • A health-related move.
  • An unforeseeable event such as death, divorce or unemployment.

Homes acquired in a like-kind (section 1031) exchange within the past five years are barred from the exclusion altogether. Two timing notes from the IRS also matter for Utah sellers. Service members and certain Foreign Service or intelligence community members on qualified official extended duty can elect to suspend the five-year test period for up to 10 years. And in an installment sale, the exclusion stays available even if you defer part of the gain.

If you end up with a capital loss on a sale that is reportable, the IRS says you can deduct up to $3,000 a year against other income ($1,500 if married filing separately) and carry the rest forward. Whether a loss on a personal residence qualifies is a question for your tax preparer, since the IRS home sale topic does not address it.

sections.h2: What federal rates apply to the taxable part?
sections.html:
Gain on a house held more than one year is long-term and taxed at 0, 15 or 20 percent federally, with a 25 percent maximum on unrecaptured section 1250 gain from real property.

Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700

Income above the 15 percent ceiling is taxed at 20 percent. A house held one year or less produces short-term gain, taxed as ordinary income. Higher earners can also owe the 3.8 percent net investment income tax, which applies when modified adjusted gross income passes $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for joint filers. Home sale gain escapes that tax only to the extent it is excluded from regular income tax.

sections.h2: How does it work if you left Utah or live elsewhere?
sections.html:
Nonresidents and part-year residents report the sale on the Utah return with Schedule TC-40B, and Utah taxes income received while you were a resident plus Utah-source income afterward.

A Utah house sold by an out-of-state owner counts as Utah-source income. Nonresidents with Utah-source income must file if they have a federal filing requirement, and they enter the full federal amount on line 4 before the schedule apportions the tax.

Utah also offers a taxpayer tax credit equal to 6 percent of a base amount that phases out as income rises, with the phase-out starting at $18,213 for single filers and $36,426 for joint filers. The capital gain transactions credit listed on the form is described as relating to certain Utah small business stock investments, so it is not a home sale break.

sections.h2: How do you report the sale and when is it due?
sections.html:
Report a home sale on Form 8949 and Schedule D, and do it even when the gain is fully excluded if you received Form 1099-S.

The IRS states that you must report the sale if you got a 1099-S or if you cannot exclude all of the gain. For tax year 2025, the Utah return and payment were due April 15, 2026. An extension of up to six months moves the return to October 15, 2026 but does not extend the time to pay, so interest and penalties can still apply.

If you sell this year, set aside the estimated tax before you spend the proceeds, and ask a CPA or enrolled agent whether quarterly estimates are needed. We can close on your timeline if you need the sale to land in a particular tax year.

faqs.q: Is there a Utah capital gains tax rate for real estate?
faqs.a: There is no separate rate. Utah taxes capital gains as ordinary income at its flat individual rate, which the 2025 TC-40 instructions list as 4.5 percent.

faqs.q: Do I owe Utah tax if the gain is under the $250,000 exclusion?
faqs.a: Usually not. Utah starts from federal adjusted gross income, so gain that is fully excluded federally does not raise the Utah taxable amount, though a 1099-S still has to be reported.

faqs.q: Does selling an inherited Utah house trigger capital gains?
faqs.a: Only on gain above the stepped-up basis. The basis is generally the fair market value on the date of death, so a sale soon after can show little or no gain.

faqs.q: What if I rented my Utah house before selling?
faqs.a: Depreciation you took after May 6, 1997 cannot be excluded and is recaptured, and gain tied to periods when the house was not your main home may also be taxable. Ask a tax professional how your rental years affect the figures.

faqs.q: Do I pay Utah tax on a house I sold from another state?
faqs.a: If the house is in Utah, the sale is Utah-source income and a nonresident must file when there is a federal filing requirement. Schedule TC-40B apportions the tax.
